articles.title: Trump says new Iran talks set to start today after calling off massive attack
articles.description: US President Donald Trump said that new negotiations with Iran will begin on Monday after he decided to hold off on striking the country to pursue a deal to end the war entering its sixth month. Trump told reporters on Sunday that the talks would cover the Strait of Hormuz — a route for global energy supplies that has become a key sticking point in the conflict —and ultimately, the denuclearisation of Iran. For its part, Iran said it was nearing a deal with Oman over a new route through the strait, where a tanker reported an explosion nearby on Sunday, underscoring the continued volatility of the strategic waterway. Oil prices fell on Monday at the opening of Asian trade after Trump announced the new negotiations, with West Texas Intermediate dropping 4.7 per cent to $80.72 per barrel. Washington and Tehran have been at war since February 28, when the US and Israel launched surprise strikes against Iran, though months of on-off diplomacy have led to periods of relative calm. Following a return to strikes last month, fears had mounted that the fighting could escalate once again. Trump had threatened to hit Iran “very hard” and was reportedly considering renewed attacks including against energy infrastructure, with US embassies across the region on alert. Trump pulled back from that threat on Saturday, saying the “parameters” of a deal were there. “Now what we’re doing is we’re talking to them in the form of a negotiation. It begins tomorrow afternoon,” Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One on Sunday, without providing details of the venue or participants in the talks. The US president said he had been asked by Iran as well as US partners Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar to hold off on the strikes, which he claimed would have been “the biggest attack since World War II”. Iranian media denied that Tehran had asked Trump not to strike. A previous ceasefire deal that included the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz fell through, and Iran has since tightened its control over the waterway. The US president said at the start of the conflict that the war was necessary to deal with Iran’s nuclear programme. Western nations accuse Iran of seeking a bomb, though Tehran insists the programme is entirely civilian in nature. ‘Exchange of views’ Iranian lawmaker Hassan Ghashghavi, spokesman for the parliament’s national security commission, said on Sunday that mediators were trying to revive the US-Iran memorandum of understanding that was agreed in June. That agreement was not intended as a final peace deal, but as a stepping stone to negotiations on a comprehensive agreement, though it did include provisions on Hormuz. “They know that the main issue and, in fact, the key to the matter right now is the issue of the Strait of Hormuz, so yes, there is an exchange of views,” Ghashghavi said. Posting on X, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said, “We must strive to compel the enemy to remain committed to what it has signed.” Iran deal with Oman? Before the war, there was free passage for all vessels through the Strait of Hormuz, but Iran closed the strait during the war and now insists on retaining control and charging tolls, something the US rejects. That dispute sparked the return to strikes last month, as Tehran refused to let ships travel any route other than one which hugs the Iranian coast. On Sunday, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei told state television that a deal was close with Oman, which sits on the other side of the strait, over a new route through it. “We are now going to reach an understanding on a route acceptable to both sides—neither the northern route nor the southern route — but one that respects the sovereign rights of both sides and safeguards our national interests and security,” he said. He insisted though that such an agreement did not mean the reopening of the strait. Maritime trade tracking firm Kpler said on Friday that traffic through Hormuz had dropped sharply. On Sunday, a tanker off the coast of Oman reported hearing an explosion near the vessel, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) Centre reported, adding that the vessel and crew were all safe.

articles.title: 'Horrific' abuse revealed after Trump DOJ drops 'botched' indictment: expert
articles.description: The Trump Department of Justice revealed something truly horrifying about itself last week after it dropped a "botched" indictment , according to one expert. Glenn Kirschner, a former federal prosecutor , argued on a new episode of his podcast, "Justice Matters," that the Trump DOJ's decision to drop its indictment against David Hearn, an Olympic canoeist, for allegedly vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool suggests that the department is in "ready, fire, aim" mode. For instance, Kirschner noted that the Trump DOJ didn't take responsibility for the facts it presented to the judge in the case. Instead, the department blamed the Department of the Interior for the information it presented. "Talk about finger-pointing," Kirschner said. "Talk about the refusal to take responsibility for your botched indictment. That is ugly. That is unseemly. As a career federal prosecutor, including decades that I served in that very office, the D.C. U.S. Attorney's Office, you don't indict first and investigate later. Nor do you take the word of another agency of government." Kirschner also noted that the prosecutor in the case, former Fox News host Jeanine Pirro, appeared to be investigating a foregone conclusion rather than applying facts to the case. "That is not the way prosecution works," Kirschner said. "Not in the 'Before Times,' but in the legal upside down [world] courtesy of Trump and Todd Blanche and Jeanine Pirro, it is ready, fire, aim, and that is inexcusable. It's horrific, and it is a gross abuse of prosecutorial discretion and power."

articles.title: "Growing pressure" as Nancy Guthrie search passes six months
articles.description: Six months after Nancy Guthrie was taken against her will from her Arizona home in the middle of the night, there are no suspects or major leads and the case seems to be stalled, a source close to the investigation tells me. "There is plenty of blame to go around, but there is growing pressure to solve this case," the source said. "This case has struck a chord — people are watching very closely. This can't go on for another six months." Savannah Guthrie, the "Today" show co-host and Nancy's daughter, wrote on Instagram on Saturday: "This is our beautiful Mom. Six months ago, someone took her out of her bed in the dead of night. We have lived every moment, every breath, and every heartbeat in agony and despair ever since." "We are begging for help," Savannah added. "We are desperate. We need someone to come forward. Someone knows something. Someone suspects something. ... Perhaps they are angry or upset for being in this situation. There is a way out - to tell what you know. You can do so anonymously. The reward is available. There is a way to end this situation and do the right thing. ... We will never stop looking for answers - and we will never stop looking for the light. ... Please. Bring her home. 💛" Between the lines: A troubling but almost overlooked aspect of the case is that the perpetrator has evaded detection in one of the highest-profile and most closely watched cases in decades. Can shrewd criminals, using the latest technology, now outfox law enforcement? Behind the scenes: A Wall Street Journal investigation published Saturday night uncovers "a trail of missteps" and finger-pointing between the FBI and Pima County Sheriff's Department. "County sheriff's deputies at first minimized the importance of dried blood found on Nancy's front porch," the Journal found. "They failed to seal off the property with police tape to protect sensitive crime-scene evidence, allowing reporters, livestreamers, and Amazon and pizza delivery drivers entry to the porch. Investigators spent precious hours deciding whether Nancy was kidnapped or lost. A search-and-rescue plane sat grounded until dusk, awaiting a deputy trained to operate its sophisticated surveillance system." The FBI told the Journal: "The state is the lead in this investigation ... The FBI has met every assistance request asked of us, even when requests came late." The FBI now may face pressure to take a bigger role, the source told me.

articles.title: 'Trump is raging': Columnist prescribes 'spinal transplant' for Congress
articles.description: President Donald Trump's erratic eruptions as Congress lay "prostrate" before him have led the United States to the "brink of catastrophe" — and it's up to voters to stop it, a furious opinion writer argued Sunday. New York Times columnist David French issued this dire warning to American voters ahead of the midterm elections, when Democrats could feasibly reclaim the House and begin checking Trump's power. "Our future may depend in part on American voters deciding to give Congress a spinal transplant," wrote French. "But that requires us to do something that democracies have rarely, if ever, done successfully — see the catastrophe coming and act decisively." The catastrophe, as French sees it, is the looming threat of World War as Trump struggles to control the situation in Iran — and himself. "Trump 'erupted' at members of his national security team over the Iran War," wrote French. "He thought he could topple a vicious, deeply embedded authoritarian regime with a few targeted airstrikes and a fantasied popular uprising." French raised alarms about Iran's continued strikes on American bases and its partners across the region, noting they may be receiving assistance from Russia and China to improve the effectiveness of their drone attacks. Iranians proved American planes and bases are more vulnerable than we realized, costs are beginning to mount and resources to dwindle, French argued. "The Trump administration has put forward two contradictory messages — that there’s no shortage of missiles in the American inventory and that the shortage is Joe Biden’s fault (because he helped to arm Ukraine and launched airstrikes against the Houthis)," French wrote. "And Trump is raging." French urged voters to sit up and pay attention rather than accept Trump assurances they can "sit back and relax." He warned the U.S. has not been so close to world war since the end of the Cold War, and argued its leaders in the White House were unfit to navigate the nation on a course to peace. "The American government is led by the worst rulers in the modern history of the United States," he wrote. "Congress, the only branch of government that possesses the power to intervene, has been prostrate before the president." French concluded that if the next Congress is not prepared to challenge Trump, there is a chance " a terrible war swallows the world."

articles.title: Electoral rolls shrink by 589,458 in less than two months as ECP removes 1.48m deceased voters
articles.description: ISLAMABAD: Pakistan’s electoral rolls contracted by 589,458 voters between May 7 and July 2, 2026, as the Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) removed a large number of deceased voters from the electoral database, more than offsetting fresh registrations during the period, it emerged on Sunday. According to official ECP statistics analysed by Dawn , the total number of registered voters fell from 137,163,857 on May 7 to 136,574,399 on July 2. A senior ECP official said 895,000 new voters were enrolled during the period, but the deletion of around 1.48 million deceased voters resulted in a net decline of 589,458 voters nationwide. The number of male voters dropped from 73,286,821 to 72,835,859, a decrease of 450,962, while female voters declined from 63,877,036 to 63,738,540, down by 138,496. The reduction narrowed the gender gap among registered voters from about 941,000 to 910,000. Overall, 99 of the country’s 144 districts recorded a decline in registered voters, while 45 districts posted a net increase. Punjab Punjab accounted for the overwhelming share of the decline. The province lost 478,909 voters, with the total falling from 77,955,543 to 77,476,634, representing 81.2 per cent of the nationwide reduction. Nine of the 10 districts with the largest declines were in Punjab. According to ECP figures, Faisalabad recorded the largest decrease, with 41,264 voter entries removed, bringing the district’s total down from 56,18,044 to 55,76,780. It was followed by Sheikhupura, with a decline of 31,783 voters, from 22,68,275 to 22,36,492; Gujranwala, with a drop of 30,302 voters, from 29,79,820 to 29,49,518; and Sialkot, which lost 30,129 voters, bringing the number down from 29,84,882 to 29,54,753. The number of voters in Gujrat dropped by 29,553, followed by Sargodha with a decline of 26,675, Multan with 26,420, Kasur with 24,367 and Bahawalpur with 22,259. Likewise, Khanewal saw a decline of 19,504 voters, Rahim Yar Khan 18,574, Lahore 16,633, Narowal 15,914, Toba Tek Singh 15,395, Rawalpindi 13,577, Mandi Bahauddin 13,480 and Attock 11,180. The number of voters in Nankana Sahib and Muzaffargarh declined by over 10,000 each. Another nine districts saw a decrease of over 5,000 each. These included Okara, which saw a decline of 9,784 voters; Khushab, 8,226; Chakwal, 7,377; Dera Ghazi Khan, 6,755; Wazirabad, 6,723; Rajanpur, 6,621; Kot Addu, 6,358; Lodhran, 6,348; and Chiniot, 5,396. Sindh Sindh recorded the second-largest provincial decline, losing 97,216 voters, with the total dropping from 28,772,963 to 28,675,747. Karachi South recorded the largest decline in the province, with 20,243 fewer voters, making it the only non-Punjab district among the top 10 districts with the biggest declines. The number of voters in the district fell from 13,30,682 to 13,10,439. It was followed by Karachi East, where the removal of 16,873 voters brought the total down from 18,15,780 to 17,98,907. Keamari lost 9,983 voters, Karachi West 8,394, Hyderabad 7,573, Khairpur 7,228 and Sanghar 6,240. KP Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) recorded a comparatively small net decline of 9,046 voters, with the provincial total falling from 23,415,995 to 23,406,949. However, it was the only province where more districts recorded gains than losses. In overall terms, the province lost 9,049 voters, accounting for 1.53 per cent of the total decline. While the number of male voters slipped by 16,884, the number of female voters increased by 7,838. Haripur lost 4,978 votes, followed by Abbottabad with 4,182, Charsadda with 3,946, Kohat with 3,352, Nowshera with 3,313, Lower Dir with 3,153 and DI Khan with 2,895. Other districts to have lost over 2,000 votes included Mardan, Hangu and Bannu. Balochistan In Balochistan, the number of voters declined by 2,226, accounting for a 0.38pc decrease. The total fell from 57,65,008 to 57,62,782, reducing the number of male voters by 6,518 while increasing the number of female voters by 4,292. Loralai and Sibi saw declines of 1,048 and 1,025, respectively. Most districts recorded marginal changes, restricted to two or three digits. Islamabad Capital Territory saw a small decline of 2,061 voters, from 12,54,348 to 12,52,287. Those removed from the electoral rolls comprised 1,118 men and 940 women. Despite the overall decline, 45 districts recorded an increase in registered voters between May 7 and July 2. KP led the gains, with 20 of its 36 districts adding voters. Of Balochistan’s 36 districts, 13 saw an increase, while nine of Sindh’s 30 districts recorded a rise in voter numbers. In Punjab, only three of the province’s 41 districts witnessed an increase in the voter count. In KP, the biggest increase was recorded in Peshawar, which added 4,835 voters, taking the total from 22,46,457 to 22,51,292. Other major gains in the province included Bajaur with 3,797, Lower Dir with 3,153, Buner with 1,738 and Mansehra with 1,603. Other districts with increases of over 1,000 included Malakand, Khyber and South Waziristan (Lower). In Balochistan, Quetta remained ahead with an increase of 4,052 voters, followed by Pishin, which saw an addition of 2,523 voters. In 11 other districts, the increase ranged between 65 and 573. Sindh also saw growth in nine districts. Karachi Central recorded the highest increase in the province, with 4,428 new voters, rising from 22,60,158 to 22,64,586. Jacobabad gained 3,928 voters, Ghotki 2,479, Naushahro Feroze 2,103 and Korangi 1,024. Other districts with nominal growth included Larkana, Malir, Tharparkar and Thatta. In Punjab, only three districts saw gains, which were offset by much larger deletions elsewhere. The largest increase was recorded in Bahawalnagar, where the number of voters surged by 16,094, from 20,12,083 in May to 20,28,177 in July, followed by Sahiwal with 4,755 and Vehari with 1,089.
